result.summary:
I fact-checked all 40 "christmas" questions in C:/Users/mleys/code_user/christmas-chaos/data/questions.json. Each xmas-NNN sits on line NNN+1. I did not edit any project file. I web-checked the doubtful facts: the Elf spaghetti scene, Clark Griswold's job, the Love Actually cue-card scene, the Jingle Bells Thanksgiving claim, snowflake symmetry, Tickle Me Elmo, where the Christmas tree started, and the 1870 holiday act.

Verdicts: 21 good, 6 weak, 4 giveaway, 4 disputed, 3 duplicate, 1 malformed, 1 wrong. The one "wrong" is xmas-025, where the answer is right but the hint shown on the TV is factually wrong. No answer is plainly wrong. The real problems are these:

(1) Giveaways. xmas-020 asks for Scrooge's first name and names him "Ebenezer" in the question. xmas-029 says "made with eggs" and the answer is Eggnog. The hints for xmas-019 and xmas-037 contain the answer.

(2) Hints shown up front. Hints appear on the TV straight away (tv.html:460-463), which makes about a third of the easy and medium questions free points. Examples: 010 "not about the sport" (Boxing Day), 013 BB gun, 017 forests and Christmas markets (Germany), 018 late 80s/early 90s, 021 Oliver Twist, 026 modern retelling of A Christmas Carol.
- **Fix:** take the hint out of the TV render by default. The host already sees the hint (host.html:631 and 635).
- Add a 'reveal-hint' socket event modelled on 'reveal-answer' (server.js:257-263), plus a state.hintRevealed flag that resets wherever answerRevealed resets (server.js:128 and 330). Give the host a "Show hint" button, and optionally halve the points once the hint is shown.
- Exception: xmas-016's "hint" explains how to count the gifts. Move that text into the question.

(3) Too many questions on the same topics.
- **Rudolph** appears in 4 questions (001, 006, 014, 039) plus sound-004. 001 even gives away 006's answer ("red-nosed").
- **A Christmas Carol** appears in 4 (008, 020, 021, 026). Christmas Vacation appears in 2 (023, 030).

(4) Duplicates with other categories. Hot Seat (server.js:93-105) draws from christmas and popculture together, so both copies can come up in one game.
- xmas-033 = pop-023 (Jingle Bells played in space).
- xmas-040 = pop-017 (the Tickle Me Elmo craze). pop-017 is itself broken: it has two "answer" keys and a garbled question.
- xmas-031's hint repeats pop-025's answer (the Thanksgiving claim, which is itself disputed).
- pop-001's hint ("Kevin McCallister...") gives away xmas-002.
- xmas-026's question text says "1988", which gives away xmas-028.

(5) Difficulty labels.
- Several "hard" questions play as medium for adults: 031, 033, 034, 035, 040.
- Several "medium" questions are easy: 019, 021, 022, 024, 027, 029.
- 008 and 014 are labelled easy but play as medium. 016, 023 and 030 play as hard.
- The `difficulty` field isn't used anywhere in the code. A search outside data/ finds no reference, and points are a flat 100 or 150 per wheel segment (server.js:19-28). Either use it (for example easy 100, medium 150, hard 200, or a badge on the TV) or drop it.

(6) Text that shows badly on the TV. xmas-038's text displays a double apostrophe ("''Twas..."). xmas-028's answer displays "1988 — and yes, the debate continues!" when the answer is revealed.

Side notes outside my category:
- pop-001 is wrong: The Grinch (2018, about $515-540M worldwide) out-grossed Home Alone (about $477M). Home Alone still leads in North America.
- Every phone receives the full question object, answer included, through spin-result and state-update (server.js:133 and publicState). Anyone could read answers in the browser's developer tools. That is minor at a family party.

Sources used: snopes.com/fact-check/jingle-bells-thanksgiving-carol; bu.edu/today/2016/jingle-bells-history; npr.org/2016/12/25/506898876; its.caltech.edu/~atomic/snowcrystals/unusual/unusual.htm; snopes.com/articles/465745/first-christmas-tree; eng.lsm.lv (Baltic tree claims); everycrsreport.com/reports/98-301.html (1870 act); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tickle_Me_Elmo; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Actually and the Fox News piece on the cue-card scene; mashed.com Buddy the Elf spaghetti recipe; catalog.afi.com/Catalog/moviedetails/58204 (Christmas Vacation); guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/102409-highest-grossing-christmas-movie; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_Christmas_films.

gaps: Christmas around the world: Sinterklaas/St Nicholas Day (Netherlands, Dec 5-6), Krampus (Austria), Iceland's 13 Yule Lads, Catalonia's Caga Tió, Mexico's Las Posadas, the Philippines' Simbang Gabi, Sweden watching Donald Duck on Christmas Eve, Ukraine's spider-web ornaments, Australia's beach Christmas, Venezuela roller-skating to Mass. The set has only La Befana and KFC in Japan.

Food and drink: mince pies, Christmas pudding and figgy pudding, panettone, stollen, bûche de Noël, tamales, Feast of the Seven Fishes, Glühwein/wassail, where candy canes come from, gingerbread houses, Christmas crackers, leaving cookies and milk for Santa and carrots for the reindeer.

Finish-the-lyric rounds for carols and songs: 'Deck the Halls' ('don we now our gay apparel'), 'Good King Wenceslas' (feast of Stephen), how many of each gift in the Twelve Days, 'Silent Night' first written in German (1818, Austria), 'Let It Snow' written during a heatwave, and mondegreens. Nothing in the set tests lyrics.

Movies by decade. 1940s-50s: Miracle on 34th Street, White Christmas, It's a Wonderful Life beyond the bell line. 1960s-70s TV specials: A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965), the Grinch cartoon (1966). 1990s: The Muppet Christmas Carol, The Santa Clause, Jingle All the Way. 2000s: The Holiday, Bad Santa. 2010s+: Arthur Christmas, Klaus, The Grinch (2018), Spirited. Also guess-the-movie-from-the-quote, and cast questions.

Christmas music charts and artists: Bing Crosby's 'White Christmas' as the best-selling single, the UK Christmas No. 1 race, 'Fairytale of New York', Mariah Carey's chart records, who sang which version, and Christmas albums.

History: Saturnalia and why December 25 was chosen, the Puritan bans on Christmas in England and Massachusetts, the 1914 Christmas Truce, the first commercial Christmas card (Henry Cole, 1843), the first electric tree lights (Edward Johnson, 1882), the real St Nicholas of Myra (modern Turkey), the 'X' in Xmas (Greek chi), and the Rockefeller Center tree (since 1931/1933).

Myth-busting true/false round: 'Coca-Cola made Santa red' (false), 'poinsettias are deadly to pets' (largely false), 'the Bible says there were three wise men' (it doesn't give a number), 'Jingle Bells was a Thanksgiving song' (unproven). This turns the set's current disputed items into a deliberate feature.

Science and numbers fun facts: female reindeer keep their antlers in winter, so Santa's team is probably female; reindeer eyes change from gold to blue in winter; Santa's required sleigh speed; how many trees are sold per year. Number questions can run as ALL PLAY 'closest wins', since ALL PLAY (server.js:26) also draws from the christmas pool.

The Nativity story and religious traditions: the Magi's gifts (gold, frankincense, myrrh), Bethlehem, Advent calendars and wreaths, Epiphany and Twelfth Night, Midnight Mass, Orthodox Christmas on January 7.

Christmas books and other origins: The Nutcracker (E.T.A. Hoffmann), The Gift of the Magi (O. Henry), How the Grinch Stole Christmas (book 1957), 'Yes, Virginia, there is a Santa Claus' (1897), Elf on the Shelf (2005), and NORAD's Santa Tracker (1955, from a misprinted Sears ad).

Hot toys and shopping by year: Cabbage Patch Kids 1983, Teddy Ruxpin, Furby 1998, Zhu Zhu Pets, Hatchimals 2016. Pick ones that adults across generations remember, and keep them from repeating facts already in popculture.
Christmas TV episodes: Friends' 'Holiday Armadillo', The Office's Christmas parties, Doctor Who Christmas specials, Mr. Bean's Christmas, The Simpsons' first episode (a Christmas special, 1989).

Easy kid-friendly tier and team-friendly formats: picture or emoji puzzles (e.g. snowman + ball emojis), 'name 5 in 30 seconds' lists (reindeer, items in the 12 Days song, Christmas movies), and family-specific custom questions. The set has no question types other than single-answer buzzer questions, and only about a dozen genuine easy ones for the youngest players.

Balance and spread: there are too many questions on Rudolph (4) and A Christmas Carol (4) and almost none on carols, food, world customs or recent (post-2010) movies. Writers should also check new questions against the popculture pool, because Hot Seat draws from both categories.

result.summary:
I checked all 25 popculture questions and all 25 sounditout songs in C:/Users/mleys/code_user/christmas-chaos/data/questions.json. Facts were checked online (Wikipedia list of highest-grossing Christmas films, Snopes, BU/NPR research on Jingle Bells, Smithsonian/Guinness on Gemini 6A, Billboard). Display behaviour was confirmed by reading the code, and the pop-017 parse result by running node. No project files were changed.

Five popculture questions have real errors:
- pop-001 is wrong. The Grinch (2018) made $552,976,825 worldwide; Home Alone made $476,684,675.
- pop-016 is a muddled question. The SpongeBob Movie is not a holiday special.
- pop-017 has two "answer" keys. JSON.parse keeps the last one, so the game shows 'What 1990s toy was at the center of a Hanukkah miracle story in A Very Rugrats Hanukkah?' and gives "Tickle Me Elmo" as the answer. That answer is wrong, and the intended question repeats xmas-040.
- pop-022 is made up ("first country to legalize Christmas trees in schools"). What actually happened: the USSR brought the tree back in 1935, but as a New Year tree.
- pop-025 states the Thanksgiving myth as fact. Snopes and BU's Kyna Hamill reject it.

Other problems:
- pop-006: the answer is right but the hint is false. Steve Jobs bought Pixar himself in 1986, not Apple.
- pop-009: the answer is written in the question.
- Hints on pop-001, pop-004 and pop-010 give the answer away. This matters because tv.html:460-463 shows the hint on the TV at the same moment as the question.
- pop-023 repeats xmas-033, and pop-025 repeats xmas-031 (whose hint even prints pop-025's answer). The Hot Seat draws Christmas and pop questions together (server.js:93-96), so these pairs can come up in the same round.

Breadth: the set does NOT meet the brief. 14 of the 25 popculture questions are Christmas questions, which overlap the 40-question christmas category. Of the 11 general ones, 6 are tech or business (iPhone, Netflix and YouTube launch years, PlayStation, Pixar, Amazon), and pop-005 and pop-011 both have the answer 2007. There are no sports questions, no music outside Christmas, nothing about games beyond PlayStation, no internet memes, nothing from the 2020s, and nothing for grandparents before 1980 apart from Brenda Lee and Tchaikovsky. Movies and TV only cover about 1990–2018.

Sound It Out has a bigger problem than its song list, confirmed by reading the code. The TV puts the song title and artist on screen for the whole room (tv.html:443-445: soundTitle.textContent = songTitle — artist, then classList.remove('hidden')). Every phone on the current team also shows the title, because isMyTurn is set per team (player.html:429, 481-483). The prompt says 'for your team to guess', yet the guessers can already read the answer, so every song is a giveaway until this is fixed.
- Fix for the TV: in tv.html:442-445, show soundTitle only when state.answerRevealed is true.
- Fix for the phones: in player.html:481, show the title only to one hummer. Either record the spinning player's socket id in server.js and compare it to the phone's socket.id, or have the host pick a hummer.
- The sounditout "hint" fields are never shown anywhere. host.html:620 puts the song title in the hint slot instead.
- The "difficulty" field is not used anywhere in server.js or the HTML.

Song quality: 13 songs are very easy to hum and recognise (001, 002, 004, 005, 006, 008, 009, 013, 015, 016, 021, 023, 025). 6 are medium (003, 007, 010, 017, 020, 024). 6 are weak (011, 012, 014, 018, 019, 022).
- Pairs that will sound alike: Silent Night / O Holy Night; Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas / The Christmas Song / White Christmas; Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree / A Holly Jolly Christmas (both Johnny Marks songs).
- Nothing is newer than 1994, so young adults only have Mariah.
- Metadata fixes: Frosty is not "Traditional" (it was written in 1950 and Gene Autry recorded it); the title is spelled "Rockin'"; the full title is "A Holly Jolly Christmas".

items.issue: Not true in unadjusted dollars. Wikipedia's List of highest-grossing Christmas films puts The Grinch (2018) first at $552,976,825 and Home Alone second at $476,684,675; Guinness also lists The Grinch. result.summary:
I reviewed all 25 dares in C:/Users/mleys/code_user/christmas-chaos/data/dares.json against the code that shows them (server.js, tv.html, host.html, player.html). I also rendered every dare on tv.html in headless Edge at 1920x1080 and 1280x720. To avoid starting the server, the script intercepts the page's requests and fakes socket.io. No text gets cut off on screen, but the render did confirm several readability problems. Scratch script, results and screenshots are in C:/Users/mleys/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/d489c8c283eb5306/1f6a997f-d385-4b62-994e-3617bc11ff4c/scratchpad/review/dares/ (render.js, render-results.json, dare-0xx-1920.png). No project files were changed.

How I used the verdicts: "good" means it can be used as is. "weak" means it works but needs a tweak to be fun or clear. "wrong" means it must be rewritten or cut before the party: it gives away its own answer, can't be judged, its scoring is broken, or it is unsafe. "duplicate" means it repeats the trivia or Sound It Out segments. "malformed" means the data itself is broken.

Totals: good 5 (001, 004, 009, 013, 016); weak 8 (002, 003, 005, 006, 007, 008, 011, 020); wrong 9 (010, 012, 014, 015, 019, 021, 022, 023, 024); duplicate 2 (017, 018); malformed 1 (025). Only about a third of the deck can be used without changes.

Problems that affect the whole deck, all confirmed in the code:

1. **No way to show a secret prompt.** Every dare's full title and description appears on the TV (tv.html:436-441), on the host screen (host.html:614-617) and on EVERY player's phone (player.html:478-479). Unlike Sound It Out (player.html:481-483), there is no check for whose turn it is. So any dare with a secret (010 movie list, 021 word list, 022 "Silent Night" in its own title, plus future charades or describe-the-gift dares) shows the answer to everyone. The screenshot dare-022-1920.png shows the answer in both the title and the description. Fix: add an optional `secret: [...]` list to the dare data. Have pickDare pick one item from it. Send that item only to the host and to the one socket that taps "I'm performing" (io.to(socketId)). The TV shows "Secret is on <name>'s phone".

2. **The `time` field is never used.** No code reads challenge.time or ch.time, and there is no countdown anywhere. Every "You have 60 seconds" depends on the host finding a stopwatch while also running the host screen. Fix: a host "Start timer" button sends `timer-start {seconds: ch.time}`, and the TV shows a large countdown.

3. **Partial scores can't be entered.** For a dare the award panel only offers +150, +50, −50 and −100 (host.html:563-569). Dares 005, 017, 018, 023, 024 and 025 ask for −10, 20 per line, −25, +25 per 10, or half points. The host can only enter those by typing a new score in the Override tab. Rule for the whole deck: every dare is pass/fail for 150, with an optional +50 crowd bonus. Also, server.js:268 doubles negative awards too, and a −50 uses up an active Double Down.

4. **Too much text to read in 5 seconds.** Descriptions run 27–47 words, which takes about 10–14 seconds to read. They sit in 20.8px text inside a 480px-wide box. The props line is 14.4px muted italic (tv.html:216-221), which can't be read from a couch. Fix: a title, one rule line of 15 words or fewer, and a "PASS:" line. Add a WHO badge (ONE PLAYER / WHOLE TEAM / WHOLE ROOM). The `type` field exists but is never used.

5. **Props.** Props are only shown once a dare comes up, so the host can't set them out ahead of time. The deck needs about 10 different prop kits (Oreos, marshmallows, a wrapping kit with oven mitts, a pillow, a cup or box with balls, candy canes, a small wrapped box, a speaker). Fix: show a props checklist on the host lobby screen.

6. **Repeats and frequency.** "Play Again" calls makeState() (server.js:343-344), which clears usedDareIds, so the second game can repeat dares from the first. Only 2 of the 12 wheel segments are dares. With 12–18 turns per game, that is only about 2–3 dares per game, so every dare has to be a strong one.

7. **Safety.** Food dares (Oreo; marshmallows contain gelatin) need an allergy or diet substitute. Jumping jacks, crawling on all fours and standing on one leg need a seated or "hold a chair" option for older relatives. Never add Chubby Bunny (a choking hazard).

items.issue: Opera carol (dares.json:69). Very funny, needs no props, and anyone can do it. The host has to come up with a carol (none are listed), and few people know a whole 'first verse'. 'Convincing' voting will be generous, which is fine for a performance dare.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = sings the full chorus/first verse in an operatic voice without breaking character (host's call, crowd cheer).
items.suggestion: Put the options on the card (no secret needed): "Sing Jingle Bells / Deck the Halls / We Wish You a Merry Christmas like an OPERA STAR. Break character = fail." Way to involve the room: "The room hums the orchestra."

items.issue: Mime the Christmas Movie (dares.json:77). The answer is visible: the 5-movie list is shown on the TV and on every teammate's phone (player.html:478-479), so the team just picks from 5 options as soon as the miming starts. 'Host picks' means saying it out loud, which everyone hears. 45 words.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = team names the secret movie within 60s with no words, sounds or mouthing from the performer.
items.suggestion: Add `secret: ["Home Alone","Elf","The Grinch","A Christmas Story","Die Hard","Frosty the Snowman","The Polar Express","Love Actually","Jingle All the Way","National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation","Miracle on 34th Street","It's a Wonderful Life"]`. Send one movie only to the performer's phone and the host. TV text: "Mime the movie on <name>'s phone. No sounds. 60s."

items.issue: Movie Quote Accent (dares.json:85). The performer has to remember a 'famous Christmas movie quote' on the spot, and many will freeze. 'Slow motion' is not an accent. A thumbs up/down vote at a family party always passes.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = delivers the quote fully in the chosen accent without breaking (host's call).
items.suggestion: Put both lists on the card: quotes "Keep the change, ya filthy animal!" / "You'll shoot your eye out!" / "Son of a nutcracker!" / "Bah, humbug!"; accents: pirate, robot, Shakespearean, sports commentator, Yoda. "The other teams shout the accent." 30s.

items.issue: Reindeer Impressions (dares.json:93). There is no goal or win condition. Everyone shouts reindeer names and the performer 'acts excited' at a 'secret' name, then nothing happens. The host can't judge it. Crawling on all fours is hard on knees and party clothes, and the secret name has no channel.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = team names the performer's secret reindeer within 30s.
items.suggestion: Rewrite as 'Which Reindeer Am I?': the performer gets a secret reindeer and a move on their phone (Dasher = sprint on the spot, Dancer = disco, Prancer = prance, Vixen = model pose, Comet = zoom around the room, Cupid = blow kisses, Donner/Blitzen = thunder & lightning, Rudolph = point at glowing nose). They act it out standing up, and the team guesses within 30s.

items.issue: 30-Second Commercial (dares.json:101). Good improv dare. The product list is fine to show (the room knowing it adds to the fun). 'Full points if the audience claps' is effectively an automatic pass.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = a 30s pitch that includes a slogan and a price (host's call).
items.suggestion: "Sell this in 30 seconds: singing Christmas tree / inflatable lawn Santa / fruitcake / Christmas Snuggie. Must include a SLOGAN and a PRICE." Optional +50 if the room gives a standing ovation.

items.issue: Christmas Rap Battle (dares.json:109). The scoring makes no sense: 'audience scores you 1–5. 30+ points = full dare points' (a 1–5 score can't reach 30, and nobody will add up the votes). It's called a 'battle' but there is no opponent. 45s of prep plus the verse goes past 90s.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = active team's rapper wins the louder room cheer in a 20s-each face-off and uses 'Santa' and 'chimney'.
items.suggestion: "RAP BATTLE: host picks a rapper from another team. 20 seconds each, must say 'Santa' and 'chimney'. Room cheers, louder cheer wins 150." No prep time. Time 60.

items.issue: Elf on the Shelf Pose (dares.json:117). 'The funniest pose (voted by other teams) wins the full 150' compares performances when only one person performs. Holding a pose for 15s is trivial, so there is no fail state.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = holds the elf pose for 30s without laughing or moving while the other teams try to break them.
items.suggestion: "Freeze in an Elf-on-the-Shelf pose for 30s. Other teams get 1 metre away and try to make you laugh (no touching). Laugh or move = fail." Gets the whole room involved and is easy to judge.

items.issue: White Elephant Reaction (dares.json:125). Funny, quick, needs no props, and the room seeing the gift is part of the joke. 'Other teams rate 1-5' has no pass threshold that matches the award buttons. 42 words; it could be shorter.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = an over-the-top happy reaction for 20–30s without cracking (host's call).
items.suggestion: "You just unwrapped: an expired coupon book / a 1-lb block of Velveeta / a novelty toilet seat. Be OVERJOYED for 30s. Crack up = fail." The host rules; optional +50 for the room's favourite.

items.issue: Speed Reindeer (dares.json:133). This is a trivia question dressed up as a dare. Trivia already has 6 of the 12 wheel segments (w0, w1, w3, w5, w7, w8 in server.js:18-31), and nothing about this is silly or physical. 'All 9' is debatable (the poem has 8; Donner/Donder). 'Each wrong answer costs 10 points' can't be tracked when a team is shouting over each other, and there is no −10 button. Most adults pass easily.
items.correctAnswer: Dasher, Dancer, Prancer, Vixen, Comet, Cupid, Donner (Donder), Blitzen + Rudolph.
items.suggestion: Cut it, or make it physical: "REINDEER ROLL CALL: teammates take turns, each says a reindeer name AND does a reindeer move. No repeats, no pauses over 3s. All 9 in 45s = pass." Drop the −10 rule.

items.issue: Carol First Lines (dares.json:141). Repeats Sound It Out: the same kind of song recall, and it would use the same carols (sound-001 Jingle Bells, sound-006 Deck the Halls, sound-007 Silent Night, sound-016 Joy to the World...). The host has no carol list on screen. '20 points per line' maxes out at 100, below the dare's 150, and can't be entered with the +150/+50 buttons. 5 carols plus announcements takes about 90s, not 60.
items.suggestion: Cut it. If song content is wanted, add a whole-room 'Finish the Lyric' question to ALL PLAY instead of a dare.

items.issue: Christmas Alphabet Blitz (dares.json:149). Impossible to judge live: the host would have to track 26 letters, 3 skips and repeats while several people shout at once. 90s is long, and it is a mental test rather than a silly one.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = team reaches letter M in 60s.
items.suggestion: "A-TO-Z RELAY: line up. Each person in turn says a Christmas word starting with the next letter (A, B, C…). Pause 3 seconds = that letter is skipped. Reach M in 60s = pass." The host only has to track the current letter.

items.issue: Gift Description (dares.json:157). A Taboo-style dare that works, but 'Host picks the gift' means the host has to invent a gift and whisper it, because the app has no list. If a list were added to the description, it would show on the TV and every phone (player.html:478-479). Needs the secret prompt feature.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = team guesses the secret gift within 30s; the describer must not say the gift name or any part of it, and no gestures.
items.suggestion: `secret: ["Ugly sweater","Fruitcake","Socks","Snow globe","Gift card","Chia Pet","Lava lamp","Air fryer","Foot spa","Selfie stick","Slippers","Board game"]`, sent to the performer's phone only. For more energy: "Get 3 in 45s".

items.issue: Spelling Bee Backwards (dares.json:165). The answer is on screen: all 5 words appear in large text on the TV (and on every phone), so the performer just reads one right-to-left. 'No writing it down!' while it's written on a TV. A spelling test is not a silly party dare, and the host has no reversed spelling to check against.
items.suggestion: Replace with a tongue twister: "Say 'Santa's short suit shrunk' 5 times fast without a slip. 20s." If kept, the word must be secret (performer's phone only) and the host screen must show the reversed spelling.

items.issue: Silent Night Miming (dares.json:173). The answer appears in both the title and the description, as screenshot dare-022-1920.png shows, so teammates read it off the TV. 'Mime the entire song from start to finish' contradicts 'identify within 20 seconds'. It also repeats Sound It Out: same mechanic (perform a song without words, team guesses) and same song (sound-007 'Silent Night').
items.suggestion: Cut it. Song-guessing already belongs to Sound It Out, and the deck needs physical or room-wide dares more.

items.issue: Ho Ho How Many (dares.json:181). Can't be counted: a fast 'hohoho' runs about 5 per second, roughly 150 in 30s, and 'other teams count out loud' turns into noise. 'Every 10 Ho's = 25 bonus' is an open-ended bonus that can exceed the 150 base and can't be entered with the buttons. There is no pass threshold. Its type is 'physical' but it is a speaking dare.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = 5+ full phrases in one breath, counted aloud by the room.
items.suggestion: "ONE BREATH: say 'Ho ho ho, Merry Christmas!' as many times as you can. The whole room counts out loud. 5 or more = pass." type 'performance', time 20.

items.issue: Christmas Freeze Dance (dares.json:189). The scoring always punishes the team: 'Last one to freeze costs the team 25 points' (×3 rounds), and someone is always last, so the active team is guaranteed −75 with no way to earn the 150. Judging who froze last is subjective, there is no −25 button, and the host has to run music on another device while using the host screen. The concept itself is great.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = at least one active-team member still standing after 3 rounds.
items.suggestion: "WHOLE ROOM FREEZE DANCE: everyone dances, host stops the music, anyone still moving sits down. 3 rounds of 15s. Anyone from the active team still standing = 150." Props: 'phone + speaker with a Christmas playlist ready'.

items.issue: Santa's Voice Reading (dares.json:197-198). The poem is stored in `props`, so the TV shows '🎒 Props needed: This text: …' in 14.4px muted italic (tv.html:216-221, 438-440, see dare-025-1920.png), which can't be read from a couch, while the instructions get the large box. The doubled apostrophe `''Twas` (dares.json:197) shows as '"Twas … Christmas''. Keeping a Santa voice for 30s is easy, so everyone passes. 'Lose half the points' (75) can't be entered with the buttons.
items.correctAnswer: PASS = reads all 4 lines in character, switching each time the room shouts, without breaking.
items.suggestion: Move the poem into a new `script` field and show it LARGE on the TV so the room reads along. Set `props: []` and fix it to "'Twas". Make it harder: "Read it as Santa. Every time the room shouts 'SWITCH!' change character (Grinch → Buddy the Elf → Rudolph). Break character = fail." Drop the half-points rule.

gaps: Whole-room participation (the biggest gap). Only 005 and 024 even involve more than the active team. Add 'other teams try to make you laugh' dares (fixed 005/015), room-counted or room-cheered dares (fixed 023/014), and whole-room freeze dance (fixed 024), so the 4–5 teams that are waiting stay involved during each dare.

Head-to-head face-offs: the active team's player vs a challenger from another team picked by the host (rap battle, oven-mitt wrap race, candy cane hook race, staring contest, 'who can hold a plank / one-leg flamingo longest'). This makes 'fastest/funniest' wording actually work and gives other teams a stake. Winner takes 150, or the challenger's team steals it.

Minute to Win It games with household props (needs a host props checklist on the lobby screen): Snowman wrap (team wraps a teammate in toilet paper as a snowman in 60s); Human Christmas Tree (decorate a teammate with tinsel/ornaments/bows); stack 6 plastic cups into a tree one-handed; flick or toss 3 marshmallows/cotton-ball 'snowballs' into a mug; carry a bauble on a spoon held in your mouth across the room; unwrap a present wearing oven mitts.

Quick-draw (needs a secret prompt): draw a Christmas thing with a paper plate on your head, or with eyes closed / your other hand, and the team guesses within 45s. Very funny and cheap: paper plates plus a marker.

Secret-prompt charades/Taboo/Heads Up dares (movie, gift, carol, reindeer, Christmas object, family tradition). They only work once the app can send a prompt to just the performer's phone and the host. Make sure each `secret` list has 12+ entries so repeats are rare.

Impressions: Santa stuck in a chimney, the Grinch discovering kindness, Buddy the Elf meeting Santa, a reindeer on its first day of flight school, 'your best impression of the host opening presents' (keep it affectionate). Short, needs no props, easy to judge.

Tongue twisters and speed-speaking to replace the spelling and alphabet dares ('Santa's short suit shrunk', 'Rudolph ran rings round red reindeer'): 5 times fast without a slip = pass. Takes about 20s and is easy to judge.
Low-mobility and seated options: every physical dare should list an option such as a seated version or 'hold a chair' for older relatives. Food dares should list an allergy/diet substitute.

Data fields every dare should have: `who` (ONE PLAYER / WHOLE TEAM / WHOLE ROOM / FACE-OFF), `rule` (15 words or fewer, shown large), `pass` (one line), optional `secret[]` and `script`, and props as a short list of real objects. Make every dare pass/fail for 150 (optional +50 crowd bonus) so it fits the award buttons at host.html:563-569. Use `type` to avoid two dares of the same type in a row.

Ideal deck size: right now about 2–3 dares come up per game (2 of 12 wheel segments × 12–18 turns), so 25 dares is plenty in quantity but full of weak ones. Aim for a curated deck of 30–40 (about 8–10 each of physical/Minute to Win It, performance/impressions, secret-prompt guessing, and whole-room/face-off). That covers 2–3 games per party without repeats and can be reused year after year. Keep usedDareIds across 'Play Again' (server.js:343-344 currently clears it) and ideally across server restarts. If the user wants silly physical moments to be a core part of the game, consider a third dare segment, or let ALL PLAY sometimes be a whole-room dare.
